lesson.title: Choosing the Right Tool: Experiments Versus Observational Studies
lesson.summary: Experiments and observational studies answer different kinds of questions, and knowing which design produced a dataset changes how strongly you are entitled to interpret its results, especially any causal claim.
lesson.body:
An observational study records data on subjects as they naturally exist, without the researcher intervening, while an experiment deliberately imposes treatments and then measures the outcome. Both are legitimate, widely used research designs, but they answer fundamentally different kinds of questions, and knowing which one produced a given dataset changes how strongly you are entitled to interpret the results.

The central tradeoff is causal strength versus feasibility. Because an experiment controls who gets which treatment, ideally through random assignment, it can balance lurking variables across groups and support a cause-and-effect conclusion. An observational study can only establish association, since any relationship it finds might be explained by a lurking variable, the same danger that produces Simpson's paradox when a confounding variable is unevenly distributed across the groups being compared. This is why a well-designed experiment with 60 subjects can sometimes provide more trustworthy causal evidence than an observational study of 60,000 people.

Consider two studies asking whether a new study technique improves exam scores. Study 1 is observational: researchers survey 500 students, ask whether they used the technique, and compare exam scores. Suppose technique users averaged 84 points and non-users averaged 76 points, an 8 point gap. But students who seek out new study techniques may also be more conscientious or better prepared to begin with, so that 8 point gap could partly or entirely reflect motivation rather than the technique itself. Study 2 is an experiment: researchers take 80 students, randomly assign 40 to learn the technique and 40 to a standard review session, then give an identical exam. Suppose the technique group averages 82 and the standard group averages 78, a 4 point gap. Because assignment was random, motivation and prior preparation should be roughly balanced between the two groups, so the smaller 4 point gap is more believable evidence that the technique itself causes an improvement, even though the raw gap is smaller than in the observational study.

Observational studies still matter enormously, especially when an experiment would be unethical, impossible, or prohibitively expensive: nobody can randomly assign people to smoke, to grow up in poverty, or to live through an earthquake, so researchers must observe those situations as they occur. Observational studies are also typically cheaper, faster, and able to use much larger and more representative samples than a controlled experiment, which is a real advantage even though the causal conclusions must be stated more cautiously.

When you compare two studies on the same question, ask three things: was the explanatory variable actually imposed by the researcher or merely observed, were subjects assigned to conditions at random, and how large and representative is the sample. A study that answers yes to imposition and random assignment earns the right to causal language such as caused or led to. An observational study, no matter how large or how strong the correlation, should be described only in terms of association, is linked to, or is related to, unless it can rule out lurking variables through other means.
